course.title: Data Analysis with Python (pandas)
course.description: Analyze real data in your browser with numpy and pandas — arrays, DataFrames, selection, filtering, and grouping — every skill practiced against automated tests, no setup required. Structure informed by the open Python Data Science Handbook by Jake VanderPlas (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 text, MIT code).

questions.prompt: What is the primary two-dimensional data structure in pandas?
questions.explanation: A DataFrame is a table of rows and columns; a Series is a single column (1-D).

questions.prompt: The numpy library is mainly used for…
questions.explanation: numpy provides efficient N-dimensional arrays and vectorized math — the foundation most data tools build on.

questions.prompt: For a DataFrame df, what does df.shape give you?
questions.explanation: df.shape is a tuple: (number of rows, number of columns).

questions.prompt: How do you select the column named 'score' from a DataFrame df?
questions.explanation: df['score'] returns that column as a Series (df.score also works when the name is a valid identifier).

questions.prompt: The pandas groupby operation is used to…
questions.explanation: groupby splits rows into groups by a key and lets you aggregate (sum, mean, count) within each group.

questions.prompt: The mean (average) of the numbers 2 and 4 is…

lessons.title: numpy arrays and pandas structures
lessons.grammar_note: A numpy array holds one data type and supports vectorized math (arr * 2 doubles every element). A pandas Series is a labeled 1-D array; a DataFrame is a dict-like collection of Series sharing an index.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what numpy arrays and pandas Series/DataFrames are, and why vectorized operations beat Python loops for data. Warm-up: if arr is a numpy array [1, 2, 3], what does arr * 2 produce?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: numpy provides the ndarray: a fixed-type, N-dimensional array with fast, vectorized operations — arr * 2 multiplies every element at once, no loop. pandas builds two structures on top of it. A Series is a one-dimensional labeled array (like a single column). A DataFrame is a two-dimensional table: a set of columns (each a Series) sharing a row index. You create a DataFrame from a dict of columns: pd.DataFrame({'name': [...], 'score': [...]}). Inspect it with df.shape (rows, columns), df.columns (the column labels), df.head() (first rows), and df.describe() (summary statistics).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: import numpy as np; a = np.array([1, 2, 3]); a * 2 gives array([2, 4, 6]); a.mean() gives 2.0; a.sum() gives 6. import pandas as pd; df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['Ana', 'Ben'], 'score': [90, 80]}); df.shape is (2, 2); list(df.columns) is ['name', 'score']; df['score'].sum() is 170; df['score'].mean() is 85.0. Selecting one row by position: df.iloc[0]['name'] is 'Ana'.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Predict each result. 1) np.array([2, 4, 6]).sum(). 2) np.array([2, 4, 6]).mean(). 3) For df above, df.shape. 4) df['score'].max(). 5) list(df.columns). Answers: 1) 12. 2) 4.0. 3) (2, 2). 4) 90. 5) ['name', 'score'].

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: looping element-by-element in Python when a vectorized numpy/pandas operation is both shorter and far faster. Mistake: confusing df.shape[0] (rows) with df.shape[1] (columns). Exit: (a) What does df.shape return? (b) What structure is a single DataFrame column? Answers: a (rows, columns) tuple; a Series.

lessons.title: Building and inspecting DataFrames
lessons.grammar_note: df['col'] returns a Series (one column). df[['a','b']] with a LIST returns a DataFrame (those columns). One bracket vs. two changes the result type.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Create a DataFrame from a dictionary and inspect its size, columns, and values. Warm-up: how many rows and columns does pd.DataFrame({'a': [1,2,3], 'b': [4,5,6]}) have?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The most common way to build a DataFrame is from a dict whose keys are column names and whose values are equal-length lists: pd.DataFrame({'name': ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Cara'], 'score': [90, 80, 70]}). The row index defaults to 0, 1, 2. Inspect it: df.shape is (3, 2); df.columns lists the labels; df['score'] is the score Series; df['score'].sum() adds it up. Select rows by position with df.iloc[0] (first row) or by a boolean condition (next lesson).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: df = pd.DataFrame({'name': ['Ana', 'Ben', 'Cara'], 'score': [90, 80, 70]}). df.shape is (3, 2). list(df.columns) is ['name', 'score']. df['score'].sum() is 240. df['score'].mean() is 80.0. df.iloc[0]['name'] is 'Ana'. df.iloc[-1]['score'] is 70. Adding a column is assignment: df['passed'] = df['score'] >= 80 creates a boolean column [True, True, False].

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For that df: 1) What is df.shape? 2) What is df['score'].sum()? 3) What is df.iloc[1]['name']? 4) What is list(df.columns)? 5) What does df['score'].max() give? Answers: 1) (3, 2). 2) 240. 3) 'Ben'. 4) ['name', 'score']. 5) 90.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: giving columns of different lengths — pandas raises an error. Mistake: expecting df['a'] (a Series) when you wanted df[['a']] (a one-column DataFrame). Exit: (a) How do you build a DataFrame from columns? (b) What does df['score'].sum() return? Answers: pd.DataFrame({...}) from a dict of equal-length lists; the total of the score column.

lessons.title: Selecting and filtering rows
lessons.grammar_note: Boolean indexing: df[df['score'] >= 80] keeps rows where the condition is True. The condition itself, df['score'] >= 80, is a boolean Series.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Filter a DataFrame to the rows that meet a condition, and count or aggregate them. Warm-up: what kind of value does df['score'] >= 80 produce?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A comparison on a column gives a boolean Series: df['score'] >= 80 is [True, True, False] for scores [90, 80, 70]. Passing that Series back in brackets keeps only the True rows: df[df['score'] >= 80] is a DataFrame of the high scorers. Combine conditions with & (and) and | (or), wrapping each in parentheses: df[(df['score'] >= 80) & (df['name'] != 'Ben')]. Count matches with .sum() on the boolean Series (True counts as 1) or len() on the filtered frame.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: df has scores [90, 55, 80, 70]. mask = df['score'] >= 80 is [True, False, True, False]. mask.sum() is 2 (two qualify). df[mask] is the two-row frame of the 90 and 80 rows. int((df['score'] >= 80).sum()) is 2. The average of the whole score column is df['score'].mean(); the average of just the high scorers is df[df['score'] >= 80]['score'].mean().

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For scores [90, 55, 80, 70]: 1) What is (df['score'] >= 80).sum()? 2) How many rows in df[df['score'] < 80]? 3) What does df['score'].mean() give? 4) Write the mask for scores above 60. Answers: 1) 2. 2) 2. 3) 73.75. 4) df['score'] > 60.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using Python's `and`/`or` between Series — pandas needs & and | with parentheses around each condition. Mistake: forgetting that a boolean Series sums to the count of True. Exit: (a) What does df[df['score'] >= 80] return? (b) How do you count the rows that match a condition? Answers: the rows where the condition is True; sum the boolean Series or take len() of the filtered frame.
